title: Which Word Carries the Water
logline: Farmers gather under a tree to decide how the tank's water will be shared for the coming season. Elders argue for how it has always been done; younger farmers argue for their own standing and results. The harvest depends on which voice wins.

object.note: Object 3 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: The wait ends on the road but continues under a tree: farmers deciding together how a tank's water will be shared, and the moment arguing facts becomes arguing standing.

thread_out.thread: The tank carries across: after the argument over its water, a village turns out to clear a bund, some because they wanted to, some because they were asked.

requirements: A village served by an ancient irrigation tank with an active farmers' organisation
A genuine water-allocation meeting occurring during the filming window
Consent from all participants, including those on both sides of the dispute

suggestions.name: A tank-irrigated farming village
suggestions.region: Anuradhapura or Polonnaruwa district, North Central Province
suggestions.why: The dry zone's ancient tank-irrigation system remains central to village farming life and organised water-sharing decisions in this region.

lesson.in_simple_terms: In a heated argument, clinging to a view and clinging to one's own standing are two different ways of holding on. The texts say they never share the same moment, so a person can switch between them without noticing.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: වාදයකදී තමාගේ මතයේ එල්ලී සිටීමත්, තමාගේ තරාතිරමේ එල්ලී සිටීමත් එකිනෙකට වෙනස් ග්‍රහණ දෙකක් බවත්, ඒ දෙක එකම මොහොතේ සිතේ නොපවතින බවත් ධර්මය කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: Among the fourteen unwholesome factors, wrong view (diṭṭhi) is grasping things other than as they are, and conceit (māna) is wrongly measuring one's own standing against others. Both grow with attachment, and both texts agree they never arise in the same moment of mind: Pradeepika because conceit is as strong as wrong view, Margaya because they are simply different kinds of grasping, one about how things are and one about where one stands.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The camera sits in the meeting under the tree through speeches, interruptions and appeals, some to how the water has always been shared and some to a speaker's own record and standing. The viewer can hear the argument drift from the water to who deserves respect, and sometimes drift back, while a season's harvest waits on the outcome.
lesson.caution: This does not mean elders appealing to tradition hold 'wrong view' or that younger farmers are conceited; wrong view in the texts is a specific mistake, and no one's mind can be read from the outside.
lesson.builds_on: Held Up showed displeasure passing through a crowd of strangers; here neighbours argue over shared water, and the lesson turns from the heat itself to the different ways a mind holds on while it argues.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
